content: Riboflavin, also known as vitamin B2, is a water-soluble micronutrient that plays a critical role in maintaining health in animals. It serves as the central component of the cofactors flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) and flavin mononucleotide (FMN), which are essential for the function of all flavoproteins. These cofactors are involved in a wide range of cellular processes. Like other B vitamins, riboflavin is crucial for energy metabolism and is necessary for the breakdown and utilization of fats, carbohydrates, and proteins. Dietary sources of riboflavin include milk, cheese, leafy green vegetables, liver, legumes (such as mature soybeans), yeast, and almonds. Riboflavin is not toxic when consumed orally, as its low solubility limits absorption to safe levels. Excess riboflavin is excreted in the urine, often giving it a bright yellow color. Toxicity is only possible with extremely high doses administered via injection, which is not typical in nutritional contexts. Industrial production of riboflavin is achieved through biotechnological methods using microorganisms such as Ashbya gossypii, Candida famata, Candida flaveri, Corynebacterium ammoniagenes, and Bacillus subtilis. Genetically modified strains of Bacillus subtilis have been developed to enhance riboflavin production and include antibiotic resistance markers for industrial use. For example, the chemical company BASF operates a facility in South Korea that specializes in riboflavin production using Ashbya gossypii. In these modified strains, riboflavin accumulates to such high concentrations that the fungal mycelium takes on a reddish-brown color and forms riboflavin crystals, which eventually rupture the cells. Riboflavin is naturally yellow or orange-yellow in color and is used as a food coloring agent and a fortifying ingredient in various food products. It is commonly added to baby foods, breakfast cereals, pastas, sauces, processed cheese, fruit drinks, vitamin-enriched milk products, and energy drinks. Riboflavin is also a key component of many multivitamin supplements, often in quantities exceeding daily requirements. The excess is excreted in the urine, leading to the characteristic bright yellow coloration. Due to its poor water solubility, riboflavin is challenging to incorporate into liquid products, necessitating the use of riboflavin-5'-phosphate, a more soluble but costlier derivative. Riboflavin deficiency, or ariboflavinosis, occurs when dietary intake is insufficient or when absorption, utilization, or retention of the vitamin is impaired. This deficiency is often accompanied by deficiencies in other vitamins. Primary deficiency results from inadequate dietary sources, while secondary deficiency may arise from conditions affecting intestinal absorption, increased excretion, or metabolic dysfunction. Symptoms of riboflavin deficiency in humans include cracked and red lips, inflammation of the mouth and tongue, mouth ulcers, angular cheilitis (cracks at the corners of the mouth), sore throat, dry and scaling skin, fluid accumulation in mucous membranes, and iron-deficiency anemia. Ocular symptoms include bloodshot, itchy, watery eyes and sensitivity to bright light. Riboflavin deficiency is classically associated with the oral-ocular-genital syndrome, characterized by angular cheilitis, photophobia, and scrotal dermatitis. In animals, riboflavin deficiency leads to growth failure, weakness, ataxia, and eventual death. Experimental studies in dogs have shown symptoms such as dermatitis, hair loss, corneal opacity, cataracts, adrenal hemorrhage, fatty degeneration of the liver and kidneys, and gastrointestinal inflammation. Post-mortem studies in riboflavin-deficient rhesus monkeys revealed significantly reduced riboflavin levels in the liver, the primary storage site for this vitamin in mammals. While overt clinical signs of riboflavin deficiency are rare in developed countries, subclinical deficiency is relatively common, affecting approximately 28 million Americans. Subclinical deficiency is characterized by biochemical changes, such as reduced erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity, and may impair growth in children. It has also been observed in women taking oral contraceptives, the elderly, individuals with eating disorders, and patients with conditions such as HIV, inflammatory bowel disease, diabetes, and chronic heart disease. Diagnostic testing for riboflavin deficiency involves measuring erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity, which reflects riboflavin status. Riboflavin has several clinical applications. For over three decades, it has been used in phototherapy for neonatal jaundice, although the treatment also depletes riboflavin levels in the infant's blood. Emerging evidence suggests that riboflavin supplementation may enhance the efficacy of beta-blockers in treating migraines. Additionally, riboflavin is being explored for its potential to improve the safety of transfused blood by inactivating pathogens. When exposed to light, riboflavin binds to nucleic acids in pathogens, breaking their DNA and RNA and effectively neutralizing them. This technology has been shown to inactivate a wide range of pathogens in platelets, red blood cells, and plasma. Riboflavin is also used in corneal collagen crosslinking (C3R) to treat keratoconus, a progressive corneal disorder. This induces collagen crosslinking, which strengthens the cornea and stabilizes the condition. In industrial applications, riboflavin's fluorescent properties under UV light make it useful for detecting leaks and assessing cleanability in systems such as chemical blend tanks and bioreactors. Good dietary sources of riboflavin include asparagus, bananas, okra, chard, cottage cheese, milk, yogurt, meat, eggs, and fish. These foods typically provide at least 0.1 mg of riboflavin per 85-300 g serving.
